The plan is honest and well-scoped, but the submission can be strengthened in several concrete ways.

1) Replace assumptions with evidence. The weakest section is market sizing and unit economics. The 8,600 markets, 30 vendors per market, and 'one third are serious' figures are acknowledged as unvalidated. Cite the USDA directory and a vendor-count source, or use the team's own local count (the 40 markets and 1,200 vendors) as the primary bottom-up basis and drop the national TAM. Also reconcile the numbers: 15% of 1,200 is 180 vendors, which at $9/month is about $19,440/year, but the plan then projects only 100 paying vendors in twelve months. Explain the gap and state which figure is the real planning case.

2) Report traction as data, not narrative. Twelve trial users and one paying vendor is meaningful early signal, but the submission gives no usage data. Add: how many of the 12 use it every market day, retention over weeks, how many sales are logged, trial-to-paid conversion so far (1 of 12, about 8%), and direct vendor quotes. Explain why the 11 non-paying trial users have not converted. That is the most important unanswered question.

3) Sharpen the problem and value quantification. The plan admits the cost is 'small per day.' Quantify it: minutes saved per market day, dollars of tax risk or penalties, bookkeeper fees avoided. A vendor must see that $9/month is clearly worth it. Also address the seasonality of income, since a flat monthly fee may cause churn in the off-season; consider seasonal or annual pricing and state the plan rather than only asking for mentorship.

4) Make the competitive section more rigorous. Name specific competitors (e.g., Square, Shopify POS, QuickBooks, Airtable-based tools), compare features and pricing in a table, and explain precisely why a farmers' market vendor would not simply use a free tier of an existing product. Acknowledge that the lack of direct card processing is a serious gap, since many vendors will want one tool for payments and records, and explain how integration (the $3,500 item) closes it and whether it affects margins or compliance.

5) Justify the funding request with milestones and metrics. The budget lines are sensible, but tie each to a measurable outcome: for example, '10 markets, 60 active vendors, 40% 90-day paid retention, measured CAC under $X.' Check whether $3,500 is realistic for payment integration, including processor fees and compliance. Define what result would justify continuing versus stopping.

6) Address the manager-report idea and drop or test it. An untested second revenue stream adds speculation. Either run two or three manager conversations before submission and report findings, or remove it.

7) Address team capacity and risk. Three full-time students at roughly 15 hours each is thin for onboarding 10 markets. Describe how time will be allocated, what happens during exams or after graduation, and whether the team intends to pursue this beyond school. Name the top risks (conversion, seasonality, incumbents adding features, sales tax rate accuracy and liability) and the mitigation for each. Note that tax guidance carries liability, so add a disclaimer and a plan for keeping rates current by jurisdiction rather than relying on manual vendor entry alone.

8) Clean up the formal gaps. Lead with a one-sentence value proposition and the key traction numbers in the first lines. Note the unformed legal entity, as is already done, but state the timeline. Add a short appendix with screenshots, interview notes, and the survey instrument. Keep claims proportional to evidence throughout; the plan's candor is a strength and should be paired with data wherever data exists.
